summary: Janes Island Light in Tangier Sound, Maryland: a light-vessel from 1854, a screw-pile house lit in 1867, ice losses in 1879 and 1936, and an unattended caisson light since 1937.

access.note: The archive lists the station as not open to the public. No source read here describes a way to visit.

events.note: Light-vessel station off the tail of Jane's bar, fixed light 30 feet above the water; the vessel was built in 1853
Light-vessels from Cape Henry southward removed or destroyed by Confederates (the report's "insurgents"); Janes Island one of the exceptions, per Lighthouse Friends
Leaking light-vessel stripped and sold at auction for $518.55
Hexagonal screw-pile house first lit night of 7 October 1867, replacing the light-vessel
Rebuilt as a hexagonal screw-pile house; light first exhibited night of 20 December 1880
Ice wrenched the fog bell from its fastenings; the bell and boat hoister were replaced from the wreck of the Solomons Lump light-house
New model fourth-order lamps installed (fiscal year ended June 30, 1899)
Keeper H. S. Moore gave assistance to occupants of a skiff caught in ice near the station (Lighthouse Friends)
Light and fog signal back in operation 14 February 1918 after ice had stopped them
Keeper L. E. Bozman assisted the disabled powerboat Secret of Crisfield near the station
Archive gives 1935 as the year discontinued; the Bulletin and the Evening Star date the destruction to February 1936 (see resolved conflicts)
Ice completely destroyed the house on 8 February 1936; keepers escaped to the mainland
New light established atop a caisson foundation
Light replaced by a 15-foot diameter steel sheet-pile cylinder with a concrete cap; light and fog signal unattended

corrections.why: The 1867 screw-pile house was destroyed by ice in February 1936 (Bulletin 1936; archive: Existing: No). The modern light is a 1937 caisson structure, which the record appears to describe.

The archive gives 38 feet (11.6 m) for the height of the light above mean high water for the 1867 house. No source read here gives 6.1 m; the modern light's focal height is not documented here. Editor should check against a current list of lights.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive gives 1935 (and Lighthouse Friends heads its entry 1935). The Lighthouse Service Bulletin for 1936 and the Evening Star of 13 February 1936 put the destruction on 8 February 1936, and Lighthouse Friends also places ice damage in February 1936. The story uses February 1936.

resolved_conflicts.field: the modern light: lit or not, and which structure is on OpenStreetMap
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's conflicts say the 1867 structure is gone but OpenStreetMap maps a point. The point matches the modern caisson light. Lighthouse Friends describes that light as shown from a caisson and unattended. No source read here confirms it is lit now.
The archive lists Alexander S. Asher as head keeper to 1945, but Lighthouse Friends says the 1937 light was unattended. No source explains the difference.
Archive: Reginald A. Peel; Lighthouse Friends: Reginal A. Peel.

notes_for_editor: Spelling: Lighthouse Friends spells the river 'Annemessic' in its 1854 entry and 'Annamessex' in 1880; the archive uses 'Annemessex'. The story uses 'Annemessex'. Keepers: the roster matches the archive's list line for line (43 lines, checked 2026-10-28); the archive compiles the National Archives keeper registers and has not been checked against the registers here. Only H. S. Moore (Commissioner's report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1917) and L. E. Bozman (Lighthouse Friends, 1928) have a second source here, and Lighthouse Friends repeats most of the archive's entries. Nancy W. Lawson (1869-1871) appears only in the archive and Lighthouse Friends; neither gives her sex, and the story does not state it. Every keeper on the list left service before about 1950, so no living-person restriction applies. Primary reports: the Light-House Board reports for 1867, 1879 and 1880 are not in the corpus (its Board volumes start in 1891), so the light-vessel, screw-pile and 1879 rebuild details are cited to Lighthouse Friends, which quotes those reports. Check them before publication. Matched by position: none in the story. OCR lines: the 1893 fog-bell item (item 455, scan page 121) is read from OCR as 'lioatiDg ice'; the story says 'by ice' and the evidence quote keeps the OCR. The 1917 keeper line 'H. S. Moore, keeper, Janes Island Light Station, Md.' (Commissioner, scan page 268, printed p. 57) is one OCR line on a page where columns run together; it is matched as a whole line, not by column position. The fact-checker did not read the page image, so check it before publication. The 1917 skiff rescue is attributed to Lighthouse Friends, which names Henry S. Moore for it. Solomons Lump is a different station, mentioned only as the source of the replacement bell and hoister. The Evening Star item is the front page of 13 February 1936 (cached page sp=1). Fiscal years: the 1899 Light-House Board report covers the fiscal year ended June 30, 1899, so the lamp installation is dated to that year, not calendar 1899; the 1917 Commissioner's report covers the fiscal year ended June 30, 1917. Disagreement on the loss: the archive gives 1935 (Year Discontinued and Disposition); the Bulletin (8 February 1936) and the Evening Star (13 February 1936) give February 1936; Lighthouse Friends heads its entry 1935 but its text gives the 8 February loss, and its next entry is 1936. The story states both. The record's characteristic (Fl W 4s), range (6 nm) and focal height (6.1 m) are not checked against a current list of lights; see corrections. Shape: the story runs to about 1,000 words with six chapters, because each chapter has sourced material. That is above the moderate row (2 to 4 chapters) and is flagged for the editor to decide whether to merge chapters.
